description: This topic explains how plants and animals exchange respiratory gases with their surroundings through specialised surfaces and structures.

mcq.questionText: What is meant by the term gaseous exchange?

options.text: The movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment
The breaking down of glucose to release energy in cells
The transport of food materials around the body
The loss of water vapour from leaf surfaces

mcq.explanation: Gaseous exchange is the process by which oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of an organism across a respiratory surface.

mcq.questionText: Through which structures does a green leaf mainly carry out gaseous exchange?
mcq.explanation: Stomata are tiny pores, mostly on the lower leaf surface, that allow gases to diffuse in and out of the leaf.

mcq.questionText: Which structures allow gaseous exchange to take place through the woody stems of older plants?
mcq.explanation: Lenticels are small openings in the bark of stems that permit gases to pass between the inner tissues and the air.

mcq.questionText: Which cells control the opening and closing of a stoma?
mcq.explanation: A pair of guard cells surrounds each stoma and changes shape to open or close the pore.

mcq.questionText: In humans, which structure separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity and helps in breathing?
mcq.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that contracts and relaxes to change the volume of the chest cavity during breathing.

mcq.questionText: What is the correct pathway of air during inhalation in humans?

options.text: Nose, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli

mcq.explanation: Air enters through the nose, passes the larynx and trachea, then the bronchi and bronchioles, finally reaching the alveoli.

mcq.questionText: Which feature of the alveoli makes them well suited for gaseous exchange?

options.text: A large, moist surface area with thin walls

mcq.explanation: Alveoli have a very large moist surface area and thin walls, allowing rapid diffusion of gases between air and blood.

mcq.questionText: During inhalation, what happens to the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles?

options.text: The diaphragm relaxes and the rib cage moves down
Both the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract
Both the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax
Only the lungs contract to pull in air

mcq.explanation: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostal muscles contract, raising the rib cage and increasing chest volume.

mcq.questionText: What structures do fish mainly use for gaseous exchange?
mcq.explanation: Fish use gills, which have many thin filaments richly supplied with blood, to take in dissolved oxygen from water.

mcq.questionText: Through which openings do insects take air into their bodies?
mcq.explanation: Insects have small openings called spiracles along the sides of the body that lead into a network of tracheae carrying air to the tissues.

mcq.questionText: Why does air breathed out by humans contain more carbon dioxide than air breathed in?

options.text: Carbon dioxide is produced as a waste product of respiration in cells
The lungs manufacture carbon dioxide from oxygen
The trachea filters carbon dioxide out of food
Carbon dioxide is added by the heart

mcq.explanation: Body cells release carbon dioxide during respiration, and this gas is carried to the lungs and breathed out.

mcq.questionText: Inside the tubes that carry air to insect tissues, oxygen reaches the cells mainly by which process?

options.text: Diffusion through the tracheae and tracheoles
Transport by haemoglobin in the blood

mcq.explanation: In insects, oxygen diffuses along the tracheae and tracheoles directly to the body cells without using blood for transport.

mcq.questionText: What is the role of the rings of cartilage in the human trachea?

options.text: To produce mucus that traps dust
To keep the trachea open so air can pass freely
To exchange gases with the blood

mcq.explanation: The C-shaped rings of cartilage support the trachea and prevent it from collapsing, keeping the airway open.

mcq.questionText: Water flowing over fish gills moves in the opposite direction to blood in the gill filaments. What is the main advantage of this arrangement?

options.text: It keeps the water warm for the fish
It maintains a diffusion gradient so more oxygen is absorbed
It removes salt from the water
It speeds up the heartbeat of the fish

mcq.explanation: This countercurrent flow keeps oxygen concentration in the water always higher than in the blood, allowing more oxygen to diffuse into the blood along the whole gill.

mcq.questionText: When guard cells lose water and become flaccid, what happens to the stoma?

options.text: The stoma turns into a lenticel

mcq.explanation: When guard cells lose water they become flaccid and straighten, which closes the stomatal pore and reduces water loss.

fib.questionText: The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment is called gaseous _____.
fib.explanation: Gaseous exchange involves the movement of respiratory gases across a respiratory surface.

fib.questionText: The tiny pores found mainly on the lower surface of a leaf are called _____.
fib.explanation: Stomata allow gases to diffuse in and out of the leaf and also permit transpiration.

fib.questionText: Gaseous exchange in the woody stems of plants takes place through openings in the bark called _____.
fib.explanation: Lenticels are loosely packed regions of the bark that let gases pass into and out of stem tissues.

fib.questionText: Each stoma is bordered by two bean-shaped _____ cells that control its opening and closing.
fib.explanation: Guard cells change shape with water content to open or close the stomatal pore.

fib.questionText: The air tube in humans that is supported by rings of cartilage and carries air to the lungs is the _____.
fib.explanation: The trachea, or windpipe, conducts air from the larynx to the bronchi.

fib.questionText: Gaseous exchange in the human lungs takes place in tiny air sacs called _____.
fib.explanation: Alveoli provide a large, moist, thin surface for gases to diffuse between air and blood.

fib.questionText: The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that helps in breathing is the _____.
fib.explanation: Contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm changes the volume of the chest cavity during breathing.

fib.questionText: Fish obtain dissolved oxygen from water using respiratory organs called _____.
fib.explanation: Gills have many thin filaments with a rich blood supply for absorbing oxygen from water.

fib.questionText: Air enters the body of an insect through small openings called _____ located along the sides of its body.
fib.explanation: Spiracles open into the tracheae, which carry air directly to the insect's body cells.

fib.questionText: The process by which gases move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration across a respiratory surface is called _____.
fib.explanation: Diffusion is the main process that moves oxygen and carbon dioxide across respiratory surfaces.

tf.questionText: Gaseous exchange and respiration mean exactly the same thing.
tf.explanation: Gaseous exchange is the movement of gases across a surface, while respiration is the chemical breakdown of glucose to release energy inside cells.

tf.questionText: Stomata are usually more numerous on the lower surface of a leaf than on the upper surface.
tf.explanation: Having more stomata on the lower surface helps reduce water loss because that surface is cooler and shaded.

tf.questionText: Lenticels are found in the leaves of plants.
tf.explanation: Lenticels are found in the bark of stems and roots, not in leaves; leaves use stomata for gaseous exchange.

tf.questionText: During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward.
tf.explanation: When the diaphragm relaxes it returns to its dome shape, reducing chest volume and pushing air out of the lungs.

tf.questionText: The walls of the alveoli are thick to slow down the movement of gases.
tf.explanation: Alveolar walls are very thin so that gases can diffuse quickly between the air and the blood.

tf.questionText: Fish can take in oxygen from water because gills have a large surface area and a rich blood supply.
tf.explanation: The thin, numerous gill filaments and good blood supply allow efficient absorption of dissolved oxygen.

tf.questionText: Insects transport oxygen to their cells using haemoglobin in the blood, just like humans.
tf.explanation: Insects carry air directly to the cells through tracheae and spiracles, so they do not rely on blood to transport oxygen.

tf.questionText: Air breathed out by humans contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than the air breathed in.
tf.explanation: Oxygen is absorbed in the alveoli while carbon dioxide from respiration is released, changing the composition of exhaled air.

tf.questionText: A good respiratory surface should be thin and moist.
tf.explanation: A thin, moist surface allows gases to dissolve and diffuse quickly across it.

tf.questionText: Guard cells open the stoma by losing water and becoming flaccid.
tf.explanation: Guard cells open the stoma when they gain water and become turgid; losing water closes the stoma.

summary.correctAnswer: The movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment.
summary.explanation: It happens across a respiratory surface by diffusion.

summary.questionText: Site of gaseous exchange in leaves
summary.explanation: Each stoma is opened and closed by a pair of guard cells.

summary.correctAnswer: Takes place through lenticels in the bark.
summary.explanation: Lenticels are loose openings that allow gases to pass in and out.

summary.questionText: Main parts of the human breathing system
summary.correctAnswer: Nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs.
summary.explanation: Air passes through these parts to reach the alveoli where gases are exchanged.

summary.correctAnswer: The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, increasing chest volume so air rushes in.
summary.explanation: Increased volume lowers the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure.

summary.correctAnswer: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, decreasing chest volume so air is pushed out.
summary.explanation: Reduced volume raises pressure inside the lungs above atmospheric pressure.

summary.correctAnswer: They are the site of gaseous exchange between air and blood in the lungs.
summary.explanation: Their thin, moist and large surface allows fast diffusion of gases.

summary.correctAnswer: Carried out by gills which absorb dissolved oxygen from water.
summary.explanation: Gill filaments have a large surface area and rich blood supply.

summary.correctAnswer: Air enters through spiracles and reaches cells through tracheae by diffusion.
summary.explanation: No blood is needed to transport oxygen to the tissues.

summary.questionText: Features of a good respiratory surface
summary.correctAnswer: Thin, moist, large surface area and well supplied with blood (in many animals).
summary.explanation: These features allow rapid and efficient diffusion of gases.

hoq.questionText: On a hot, dry afternoon a plant closes most of its stomata. What is the most likely benefit and trade-off of this response?

options.text: It reduces water loss but also slows gaseous exchange and photosynthesis
It increases water loss but speeds up photosynthesis
It stops respiration completely in the roots
It allows lenticels to take over photosynthesis

hoq.explanation: Closing stomata conserves water during heat, but it also limits the entry of carbon dioxide, reducing gaseous exchange and the rate of photosynthesis.

hoq.questionText: A fish taken out of water soon suffocates even though the air around it is rich in oxygen. Which explanation best fits this observation?

options.text: Air contains no oxygen that fish can use
The gill filaments stick together and collapse, reducing the surface area for gaseous exchange
The fish stops respiring as soon as it leaves water
Oxygen in air is too cold for the gills to absorb

hoq.explanation: Out of water the wet gill filaments dry and clump together, drastically reducing the moist surface area, so too little oxygen can diffuse into the blood.

hoq.questionText: Why can very large active animals not rely on the simple tracheal system used by insects for gaseous exchange?

options.text: Because diffusion alone through tubes would be too slow to supply oxygen deep inside a large body
Because large animals do not respire
Because spiracles can only open in cold weather
Because tracheae are made of bone in large animals

hoq.explanation: Diffusion is efficient only over short distances, so large active animals need lungs or gills with a transport system to carry oxygen quickly to deep tissues.
